passage:
The garden-plot booking site Emil's team had built for the Copenhagen library went live on Monday. By Wednesday only forty people had signed up, and Emil told Abebe over coffee, "It's a total failure. Six months, wasted."
Then he heard himself. Total? He pulled a napkin over and drew a line from one to ten. "Okay. Where does it really sit?"
Abebe shrugged. "Five? Maybe six?"
They made two columns. Worked: the booking system never crashed; older users liked the big buttons; the librarians loved the reports. Didn't work: nobody knew it existed, and sign-up took too many steps.
Emil stared at the napkin. "So it's a decent product nobody's heard of."
"That's a very different problem," Abebe said. "And a fixable one."

qa.q: How many people had signed up by Wednesday?
qa.a: Forty people.

qa.q: What was Emil feeling when he called the project a total failure?
qa.a: Emil felt deflated and discouraged, as if six months had been wasted, until he caught the word "total".

qa.q: What made Emil's napkin exercise useful?
qa.a: Rating the project on a scale and listing what worked and what did not turned "failure" into specific, fixable problems 👍: nobody knew about it and sign-up was too long.

qa.q: How does Abebe see the project?
qa.a: Abebe sees a middle result, five or six out of ten, and points out that a decent product nobody has heard of is a fixable problem.

grounding: An adult who called a project a total failure rates it on a scale and lists what worked and what did not.

passage:
On the village bus the morning after Bohag Bihu, Simran realised her maths notebook was still at home, under the pile of new gamosas. Her chest went tight. Ma'am will shout, she thought. Then she'll hit my hand with the ruler. Then she'll call Deuta. Then they'll throw me out of school, and everyone in the village will know, forever.
"Simran, why are you crying?" asked Binita, her friend from the next seat.
"I forgot my homework and now my whole life is finished."
Binita blinked. "Last week Rupam forgot his. Ma'am just said bring it tomorrow."
Simran wiped her nose. It didn't feel like it could be that simple.

qa.q: Where was Simran's maths notebook?
qa.a: At home, under the pile of new gamosas.

qa.q: Why did Simran say her whole life was finished?
qa.a: She felt panicky and ashamed 😰, and her mind leapt from a forgotten notebook to the worst possible ending, each step feeling real.

qa.q: What could help Simran when her mind races like this?
qa.a: Stop and ask what really happened last time someone forgot, as with Rupam, and plan one small step, such as telling Ma'am and bringing it tomorrow.

qa.q: How does Binita see Simran's worry?
qa.a: Binita is surprised, because she has seen Ma'am calmly say "bring it tomorrow", so the disaster seems far bigger than the problem.

grounding: A child who forgot her homework imagines being punished, expelled and shamed forever, leaping to the worst ending.

passage:
It was the first hot night of summer in Valencia, and fireworks for San Juan were already cracking over the beach. At six, Ines had sent Javier a photo of her new haircut: "thoughts?? 😬" It was now nine. The two grey ticks just sat there.
At seven she decided he thought it looked terrible. At eight she decided he was laughing about it with Lucía. By nine she was sure the whole group had a chat without her, and that on Monday everyone would look away. Her stomach churned. She typed "forget it, I know it's ugly" and hovered over send.
Then her phone buzzed. "sorry!! at my abuela's, no signal till now. it looks amazing 😊"
Ines let out a breath she hadn't known she was holding.

qa.q: When did Ines send Javier the photo?
qa.a: At six.

qa.q: What was Ines feeling as the hours passed?
qa.a: She felt anxious and afraid; each imagined step, that he hated it, that he was laughing, that everyone hated her, felt certain when it was only fear.

qa.q: What could Ines try next time a reply is slow?
qa.a: Remind herself of ordinary reasons such as no signal, hold off on drafting hurt messages, and wait for facts before believing the worst.

qa.q: How might Javier have felt if Ines had sent "forget it, I know it's ugly"?
qa.a: Javier would probably be confused and a bit hurt, since the only reason for the silence was having no signal at his abuela's.

grounding: A teenager whose friend has not replied builds a chain of fears until she is sure everyone hates her.

passage:
It was the week before Christmas, placement season, and the campus was strung with fairy lights I couldn't stand to look at. I'd just come out of the first interview of the season, where I froze on the second coding question.
Walking back, my mind ran ahead like a train. They'll reject me. Then every company will. I'll be the only one in the batch without a job. Papa took a loan for my fees; I'll never repay it. Everyone at home will whisper. By the hostel gate I'd reached "failure at thirty".
Gopika found me on the steps. "Omkar, what happened?" I told her the whole chain. She said, "Okay. What actually happened in the last hour?"
"I froze on one question."
"And?"
Said out loud, the chain looked ridiculous. One interview. Twelve companies still to come.

qa.q: What happened to Omkar in the interview?
qa.a: Omkar froze on the second coding question.

qa.q: Why did Omkar's thoughts race all the way to "failure at thirty"?
qa.a: Omkar felt anxious and ashamed after freezing, and each fearful step felt like logic while skipping everything in between.

qa.q: What question helped break the chain, and why?
qa.a: Gopika asking what actually happened in the last hour brought Omkar back to one fact, one frozen question, with twelve companies still to come.

qa.q: How might Gopika see Omkar on the steps?
qa.a: She sees a friend overwhelmed by a single bad interview and responds calmly, helping separate the facts from the fears.

grounding: A final-year student who froze in one interview pictures never being employed and shaming the family, until a friend asks for the facts.

passage:
Let me tell you something, since you're panicking about that typo. When I was new at the bank, maybe twenty-five, my deskmate Swati found a wrong date in a report she had already sent to the regional office. She went white. "That's it. They'll think I'm careless. I'll lose my confirmation. I'll have to go back home." Her hands were shaking.
I didn't tell her to calm down; that never works. I asked, "Swati, what's the worst thing that could realistically happen?"
She thought. "My manager emails me."
"And how likely is it they sack you over a date?"
She almost laughed. "Not very."
We sent a one-line correction. The reply said, "Thanks, noted." That was all. Tenzin's rule, I call it now: ask the worst realistic question before you believe the worst imagined one.

qa.q: What mistake did Swati find in the report?
qa.a: A wrong date.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling while Swati spiralled?
qa.a: Tenzin felt concerned but steady, knowing that "calm down" would not work and choosing careful questions instead.

qa.q: What turning point shrank the disaster?
qa.a: Asking what the worst realistic outcome was and how likely it was, which led to a one-line correction and a simple "Thanks, noted."

qa.q: What was that moment like for Swati?
qa.a: Swati felt frightened and ashamed, sure the error would end her career, until the questions let her see how small it was.

grounding: A colleague sees a peer treat a small report error as career-ending and asks about the worst realistic outcome and its likelihood.

passage:
The notice went up on Monday: a big electronics showroom would open across the road from Eshaan's little repair shop in Ranebennur. That night he couldn't sleep. Customers will go there. I'll lose the shop. I won't manage the rent.
Manjula, his wife, found him awake at two and handed him a notebook. "Write it, then."
He wrote: Fear: nobody comes. Below that: How likely? The showroom sells new phones; it doesn't fix old ones. Some customers may go. What could I do? Offer quick repairs they can't. Put up a board: "Bought it there? Fixed here." Ask the showroom to send repairs my way.
By three the page held six options instead of one ending. He switched off the lamp. "It's still scary," he said. "But now it's a list."

qa.q: What was going to open across the road from Eshaan's shop?
qa.a: A big electronics showroom.

qa.q: What was Eshaan feeling before he started writing?
qa.a: He felt helpless dread, unable to sleep, jumping straight to losing the shop.

qa.q: How did the notebook change things?
qa.a: Writing the fear, how likely it was and what he could do turned one frightening ending into six options, such as quick repairs and a board for showroom buyers.

qa.q: How might Manjula see that night?
qa.a: Manjula sees her husband's worry and responds practically with a notebook, and is probably relieved when the page fills with options.

grounding: An adult writes down a feared outcome, how likely it is and what he could do, turning dread into options.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Christmas play week.
Today Vinita stopped coming to rehearsal to watch. When I asked why, she said, very certainly, "You think I'm useless. That's why you didn't give me a part." She said it like a fact she had read somewhere.
In truth I had picked names from a bowl, because twenty-two children wanted eleven roles, and I had planned to ask her to narrate next term's play because she reads beautifully. Anand, who also wasn't picked, told her it was a lottery, but she shook her head.
Next step: I showed her the bowl with the leftover name slips and asked if she would help with the stage lights this week. She agreed, but she is still watching my face very carefully.

qa.q: How did the teacher choose who got parts?
qa.a: By picking names from a bowl, because twenty-two children wanted eleven roles.

qa.q: Why did Vinita say the teacher thinks she is useless?
qa.a: She felt hurt and rejected at not getting a part, and her guess about the teacher's thoughts felt like certain fact without any evidence.

qa.q: What did the teacher do, and what else could help?
qa.a: Showing the bowl and offering the stage-lights job gave evidence against the belief; telling Vinita about the narrator plan could help further.

qa.q: How does Anand see not being picked?
qa.a: Anand sees it as a lottery, not a judgement, which is why he tries to tell Vinita so.

grounding: A child not chosen for the class play decides the teacher thinks she is useless and states it as fact.

"You clearly hate the plan," Leela said, pushing the laptop away. The monsoon was hammering the canteen roof, and they had been planning the Onam trip to Munnar for an hour.
"What? No."
"You've said three words in twenty minutes. You're sitting like this." She crossed her arms dramatically. "Just say it, Tarun. You don't want to come."
Tarun rubbed his eyes. "Leela, I was on night shift at the call centre till six this morning. I'm not angry. I'm just wrecked."
"Oh."
"I actually love the houseboat idea. I just can't think in full sentences right now."
Leela pulled the laptop back, a little sheepish. "Okay. Houseboat, yes. We'll do the rest tomorrow when you're human?"
"Deal. Wake me if I snore."

qa.q: Where had Tarun been until six that morning?
qa.a: On night shift at the call centre.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling when Leela said he hated the plan?
qa.a: Tarun felt misread and exhausted, not angry; he was simply too tired to talk much.

qa.q: What did Tarun do that cleared things up?
qa.a: He gently said what he was actually feeling, wrecked rather than angry, and that he loves the houseboat idea.

qa.q: How does Leela feel once she hears the reason?
qa.a: Leela feels a little sheepish for assuming, and relieved 😅, agreeing to finish the planning the next day.

grounding: A tired, quiet student is told he clearly hates the plan and gently explains what he is actually feeling.

passage:
I sit between Joseph and Tanuja, so I saw the whole thing. On Tuesday Tanuja answered Joseph's message with just "ok." No emoji, no thanks. Joseph read it and went stiff. For the next hour he kept glancing over, rewriting an email and muttering, "She's annoyed about the budget slides. I should have checked with her." He even drafted a long apology. I can't say what was in his head, but he looked miserable.
Then, around four, he simply walked over. "Tanuja, quick one. Is something wrong? Your 'ok' sounded annoyed."
She looked up, confused. "What? No, I was typing with one hand, eating lunch." They both laughed. The whole thing took two minutes.
Joseph came back and deleted the apology. "Reena," he told me, "I just spent three hours arguing with a Tanuja who doesn't exist."

qa.q: What did Tanuja reply to Joseph's message?
qa.a: "ok."

qa.q: What was Joseph feeling after reading the short reply?
qa.a: He felt anxious and guilty, sure Tanuja was annoyed about the budget slides, and spent hours imagining her anger.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Walking over and asking directly whether something was wrong 🙂; a two-minute question replaced three hours of imagined arguments.

qa.q: How does Tanuja experience Joseph's question?
qa.a: She is surprised and confused at first, then amused, since her short "ok" was only one-handed typing at lunch.

grounding: An adult sure that a colleague is annoyed asks her directly and finds the imagined anger was never there.
